Apple’s iPhone didn’t just grow—it pulled the whole smartphone market into an upgrade-cycle vortex. While Samsung fought pricing pressure, Huawei got crushed by restrictions, and Xiaomi struggled to sustain momentum globally.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The iPhone Upgrade Spiral: how Apple’s phones pulled the market into a money-making machine

For years, smartphone growth looked like a flatline battle—until “upgrade cycles” turned into a weapon. In 2019, Apple’s iPhone revenue sat at $142.4B, already massive, but not yet the unstoppable force it would become. Then 2020 hit—iPhone dipped slightly to $137.8B—while the world reset what “premium” meant.

The real plot twist started in 2021. Apple’s iPhone revenue snapped upward to $191.9B. That’s not a tiny gain—that’s a jump big enough to redraw charts. In 2022, it stayed elevated at $205.5B as Apple doubled down on ecosystem stickiness (services + device lock-in + resale value dynamics). Even when the broader market cooled, iPhone kept its grip: $200.6B in 2023 and $215.8B in 2024.

Now look at the contrast cast. Samsung Mobile peaked higher earlier, hitting $216.9B in 2020, then gradually slid: $221.0B in 2021, down to $210.6B in 2022, $196.3B in 2023, $185.0B in 2024, and an estimated $178.0B in 2025. The message? Price pressure and product cycles became harder to defend.

And Huawei… Huawei’s story is the collapse chapter. Revenue went from $122.9B (2019) to $98.0B (2020), then cratered to $32.2B (2021) and basically fell off the chart afterward—down near $0.8B in 2022 and about ~$0.4B by 2024–2025. Meanwhile Xiaomi stabilized in the low-to-mid tens of billions: $22.4B in 2019, $31.6B in 2021, hovering around $30B-ish through 2024–2025.

Question for you: In a “slow upgrade” world, is the real winner the phone specs… or the ecosystem gravity? Drop your take 👇 and follow for more viral timeline chart-races.
facebook_caption:
Apple’s iPhone revenue demonstrates how upgrade cycles and ecosystem lock-in can overpower normal smartphone competition. In 2019, Apple generated $142.4B from iPhone sales, slipping to $137.8B in 2020 before accelerating sharply to $191.9B in 2021.

The momentum continued: iPhone revenue reached $205.5B in 2022, remained resilient at $200.6B in 2023, and climbed to $215.8B in 2024, with an estimated $220.0B in 2025. Meanwhile, Samsung Mobile peaked around the 2020–2021 period ($216.9B in 2020; $221.0B in 2021) and then declined through 2025 ($178.0B estimated), reflecting intensifying competition and pricing pressure.

Huawei provides the most dramatic counterpoint. After $122.9B in 2019 and $98.0B in 2020, revenue dropped sharply to $32.2B in 2021 and fell to roughly $0.8B in 2022 and about $0.4B by 2024–2025, consistent with the market impact of trade restrictions.

Xiaomi remains the smaller but steadier comparator, rising from $22.4B (2019) to $31.6B (2021) and then stabilizing near ~$30B through 2024–2025.

Net takeaway: ecosystems plus timing can create outsized revenue trajectories even when the broader market matures.
threads_caption:
Apple’s iPhone is basically the case study for “ecosystem > specs.” 📱

From $142.4B (2019) → $137.8B (2020) → then WHOOSH: $191.9B (2021) → $205.5B (2022) → $215.8B (2024). Even into 2025 it’s still around $220B.

Meanwhile Samsung peaked around $216.9B (2020) and slid toward ~$178B by 2025. Huawei went from $98B (2020) to basically nothing (~$0.4B by 2024–2025). Xiaomi stayed in the ~$20B–$33B lane.

So yeah: upgrade cycles + ecosystem stickiness really matter. Do you think Apple’s advantage is mostly hardware… or mostly the ecosystem?
